questions.q: What is the primary role of hormones in the human body?
questions.a: Hormones act as chemical messengers that travel through the bloodstream to give instructions to specific body tissues. A student who says "hormones are food for growth" misses the point that they are *signals*, not nutrients.

questions.q: If hormones are produced in one part of the body, how do they reach the part of the body that needs to grow?
questions.a: They travel through the bloodstream, which acts like a highway system for these signals. A student who thinks hormones travel through nerves or by "magic" fails to understand the circulatory system's role as a delivery mechanism for chemical messengers.

questions.q: Why is the gland at the base of the brain often called the "master conductor"?
questions.a: It sends out the initial signals that tell other glands in the body to start releasing their own hormones. If a student answers "because it is the biggest gland," they are confusing size with function.

questions.q: If you were to compare the body to a school, what would the hormones be?
questions.a: Hormones would be the "announcements" or "instructions" sent from the Principal's office (the brain) to the classrooms (the tissues). A student who confuses the hormones with the "students" themselves doesn't grasp that hormones are merely the message, not the physical change itself.

questions.q: Can a change in adolescence happen without a chemical signal from a gland? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because the body requires these specific chemical instructions to initiate the maturation process. A student answering "yes" suggests they believe these changes are automatic or accidental rather than biologically programmed.

questions.q: Design a simple analogy to explain to a friend how a hormone works.
questions.a: A good answer would use an analogy like a letter sent via the post (bloodstream) to a specific house (tissue) to tell the resident to start a new task. A poor answer would be too vague, such as "hormones make you grow," without explaining the *signal-delivery-response* process.
